sentences.text: From question to publication with the Enobio 8: frontal alpha asymmetry during video commercials
This workshop follows one advertising question from a client's first sentence to a written results and discussion section.

You will plan a test of two versions of one commercial and a second commercial, build it in iMotions Lab 11 point 1, fit an electroencephalography (E E G) cap on a viewer's head, turn the brain's electrical rhythms into a frontal alpha asymmetry score, test three hypotheses, and write the result for a journal and a client.
Every section explains why before how.
E E G records the brain's electrical activity from the scalp.

Each electrode, a small sensor held against the scalp by a cap, picks up tiny voltage changes from many neurons firing together, typically within 100 microvolts (millionths of a volt) of the mean, each measured against a reference site such as an ear.
The lab's Enobio 8 takes 500 samples per second, a sampling rate of 500 hertz (lab manual).
The trace is a mixture of rhythms.
A frequency band is a range of them, counted in hertz (hertz), cycles per second.

The iMotions notebooks use delta (1 to 3 hertz), theta (4 to 7 hertz), alpha (8 to 12 hertz), beta (13 to 25 hertz), and gamma (26 to 40 hertz); the iMotions introduction to E E G gives slightly different limits (delta 1 to 4, theta 4 to 8, gamma above 25 hertz), so a report always names the bands it used.
A band's strength is its power (section 06).
This workshop uses alpha, because "Alpha power is inversely related to the level of brain activity in the alpha range" (iMotions notebook article): where the cortex works harder, alpha falls.

Frontal alpha asymmetry (F A) takes the natural logarithm (natural log, which turns a ratio of two powers into a difference) of alpha power at a right and a left frontal electrode and subtracts left from right, so a positive or rising score means relatively more activity on the left.
That pattern is read as approach motivation, the pull toward something, and the reverse as withdrawal motivation, the pull away.
The scores "should be interpreted relative to each other," so each viewer is compared with his or her own resting baseline, never with zero.
Three limits run through every section.
F A shows a balance of motivation, not which emotion a person feels; it does not show liking or buying by itself; and it cannot time events to the millisecond.

An event related potential (E R P), the small voltage wave that follows a repeated event at a fixed delay, needs trigger hardware, while the lab mostly relies on software synchronization, where "the precision of the iMotions software is in the range of tens of milliseconds."

The lab owns one Neuroelectrics Enobio 8: a neoprene cap in three sizes, eight electrodes, conductive gel and blunt syringes, reference and ground leads labeled C M S and D R L (on an ear clip, or placed close together without touching), and a U S B adapter.
Sites follow the ten ten system: a letter for the region (F for frontal), odd numbers left, even numbers right, z on the midline, so F 3 and F 4 are a left and right frontal pair.

N I C 2 (Neuroelectrics Instrument Control) shows each electrode's contact and sends the signal through Lab Streaming Layer (L S L) into iMotions, where the E E G R Notebooks, analysis scripts built into iMotions, compute F A.
The worked example is DEMO - Sony Bravia, with a simulated data set of 48 respondents.
Time needed.
About 5 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (planning, building, recording) in the first, 06 to 10 (analysis and writing) in the second
Equipment.

The Enobio 8 kit (cap in Small, Medium, and Large, eight electrodes, gel and blunt syringes, the ear clip or the C M S and D R L leads, the U S B adapter), a tape measure for the head, and the lab computer
Software.
N I C 2 and iMotions Lab 11 point 1 with the E E G module, Lab Streaming Layer, and the E E G R Notebooks, plus R or Excel for section 08
Data files.
The simulated E E G files in the site's data folder (exports, artifact report, session log, survey, analysis dot R, Excel workbook), plus DEMO - Sony Bravia in the lab Library
How to use.
Work top to bottom, answer each quick check, then tick the section
You need a lab computer with N I C 2 and iMotions Lab 11 point 1, the Enobio 8 kit, and this page, but no earlier workshop.
The statistics you need are a mean, a standard deviation (how far a typical value sits from the mean), and the idea that a test asks whether a difference is larger than chance would produce.
Terms with a dotted underline open a definition when you tap them.
Help center links open after you sign in through my dot imotions dot com; for a longer introduction, read Introduction to: E E G.
At a lab computer, open iMotions in another window to follow the screens in sections 04, 05, and 07.
Nothing in this workshop records into, deletes, or changes the lab's existing studies; open DEMO - Sony Bravia only to look.
The one sentence this workshop keeps repeating Before the first respondent sits down, write down which scalp site each of channel 1 to channel 8 holds.
The Enobio names its channels only channel 1 to channel 8; the N I C 2 protocol decides the sites.
The notebook's Enobio default is left channel 1 and right channel 7.

Under the lab manual's example montage, the sites in channel order (F z, C z, P z, O z, F 3, F 4, P 3, P 4), those are F z and P 3, and the defaults would give a normal looking number that means nothing; F 3 and F 4 would be channel 5 and channel 6.
The map is assumed until read on the lab computer, and the electrode sets are entered by hand in every F A analysis.

Say what E E G and frontal alpha asymmetry measure and what they cannot, name the five frequency bands, explain why a rising F A score means relatively more left frontal activity, and list the equipment, software, and files this workshop uses.
From idea to research question
A client rarely arrives with a research question, only a business question.

Picture a brand team with a finished commercial built around one striking moment, the key scene, that asks (a teaching scenario modeled on the iMotions demo study, not a statement about any brand): "Does the key scene in our commercial make people want the brand more?"
The sentence names a scene and a wish, but not who will watch, what "want" means, how it will be measured, or what difference would count.
A research question names the problem the study will answer and signals the type of study needed; a hypothesis is a testable answer to it, written with the variables that will be measured.
First, though, you need to know what a cap of electrodes can say about wanting.
Researchers who study the frontal cortex describe motivation as running from approach motivation, the urge to move toward something, to withdrawal motivation, the urge to move away.
A long line of E E G research links relatively greater left frontal activity to approach and relatively greater right frontal activity to withdrawal.
Reviews treat frontal asymmetry both as a stable trait that differs between people and as a state that shifts with what a person faces.
An advertising study asks about the state: did the balance move during this scene?
Approach is not the same as liking.

Valence is whether a feeling is pleasant or unpleasant, and the two can part company: anger is unpleasant, yet it pulls a person toward its target, and it goes with relatively greater left frontal activity, like other approach states.
The iMotions notebook article agrees: "these motivational systems operate independently of valence."

Some iMotions texts add the words liking and disliking in parentheses after approach and withdrawal; this workshop keeps the motivational words, and section 06 returns to an iMotions article that reads otherwise.
What frontal asymmetry can answerDid the key scene shift a viewer's frontal balance toward approach, compared with the same viewer at rest a minute earlier?
Was the end of the commercial, where the brand appears, met with more approach after the version with the key scene than after the version without it?
Which of two commercials shifted the balance more?
What it cannot answerDid viewers like the scene or the brand?
Which emotion did they feel: delight, curiosity, or irritation?
Will they buy?
Each needs another measure: a rating, facial expression analysis (Workshop 3), or a criterion such as choice or sales.
Reading a specific mental state, such as liking, straight off a brain signal is called reverse inference, and it holds only to the extent that the signal is specific to that state.
F A is not specific to liking.

Of the lab's measures it is the closest to the client's word "want," because wanting is a pull toward something, but a shift toward approach during a scene is not a purchase, and it is not even a response to the brand unless the brand is on screen.
Why measure approach in advertising?
The demo this workshop follows was inspired by a study that compared Sony Bravia commercials with frontal alpha asymmetry (Ohme, Reykowska, and colleagues
, 2010), and a companion article discussed the frog scene in one of them, Balls.
The same group had recorded E E G and skin conductance during two versions of a skin care advertisement (Ohme and colleagues
, 2009), and a review covers E E G and related tools in neuromarketing.

Prediction of the market is a separate question: brain responses to movie trailers predicted individual preferences and the films' population wide commercial success; how similarly viewers' brain activity unfolded over time predicted audience preferences (Dmochowski and colleagues
, 2014); and one study combined neurophysiological methods with market response modeling to ask which measures predict advertising success beyond traditional ones.
F A is evidence about motivation during a scene, not a forecast of sales.
Now the hypotheses, written before any data exist.

The independent variables, what the researcher changes, are the period (a resting baseline, a neutral 60 seconds nature video just before each commercial, or a segment of the commercial), the version of Commercial 1 (Version A with the key scene, Version B with it cut), and the commercial (Commercial 1 or Commercial 2).
The dependent variable is Mean Frontal Asymmetry Alpha, the notebook's mean F A over a stimulus or marked segment, taken as a change score: the segment minus the baseline just before its commercial.
The end scene is the last 10 seconds of each commercial, where the brand appears, the window the demo study analyzed.
Among viewers of Version A, F A during the key scene is higher than F A during the baseline before the commercial.
The baseline corrected F A during the end scene of Commercial 1 is higher after Version A, with the key scene, than after Version B, without it.
The baseline corrected F A over the whole commercial differs between Commercial 2 and Commercial 1.
Exploratory.

How the F A change relates to a liking rating (1 to 7) after each commercial; recall of the key scene and the brand; and frontal midline theta, theta power at the midline frontal site F z, which rose with task load in the workload study iMotions cites (M.
E. Smith and colleagues, 2001).
A two tailed test asks whether two means differ in either direction; a one tailed test looks only in the predicted direction and is blind to a difference the other way.
All the tests here are two tailed, but a hypothesis may still state a direction if a reason is written down before the data, and then it counts as supported only when significant in that direction.
H 1 states one because the scene was made to draw viewers in, and the published Sony Bravia work singled out one scene, the frog, for analysis with E E G.
H 2 states one because approach raised by the key scene may carry into the end scene, where the brand appears; it can fail even when H 1 holds.
H 3 states none: the commercials differ in everything at once, and nothing known beforehand says which should draw more approach.
The demo's chart favored one commercial, but four respondents are an anecdote, and this plan's commercials are not the Sony ones.
Now the client's sentence can be rewritten.
The lab asks every study to pass through one sentence with four slots: who, sees what, measured how, compared against what.

Here: adult viewers (who) watch one version of Commercial 1, assigned at random, and Commercial 2, each after its own 60 seconds baseline, in a balanced order (sees what), while an Enobio 8 cap records E E G and a rating slide asks how much they liked each commercial (measured how), and each segment is compared with the same viewer's baseline, the versions with each other, and the commercials with each other (against what).
Weak questions fail in their own ways.
"Does the key scene work?"
asks for a judgment: work at what?
"Do viewers love it?"
asks about valence, "What do people feel?"
asks which emotion, and "Will it sell?"
asks about the market.

The repair names an observable, a window, and a comparison: "Among viewers of the version with the key scene, does frontal alpha asymmetry during the scene rise above each viewer's own baseline, and is the end scene met with a larger shift toward approach after that version than after the version without the scene?"
It claims a shift toward approach, not wanting the brand, and certainly not buying it.
The last step is to choose one primary measure for each hypothesis before the data exist and to label everything else exploratory.
The notebooks report asymmetry in five bands and power at every channel and band, for every stimulus and segment; test them all and something will come out by chance.
Here the primary measure is Mean Frontal Asymmetry Alpha as a change from the preceding baseline, in one window per hypothesis: the key scene, the end scene, the whole commercial.
Filing that plan before collection is called preregistration; it lets a reader tell a prediction from a story told afterward, and section 08 holds you to it.

Turn a client's question about wanting a brand into a testable research question, separate approach motivation from liking and valence, say what frontal asymmetry can and cannot support, and write three hypotheses with one primary measure and window each, with no direction where none can be defended.
Designing an E E G ad study
A frontal asymmetry study of a commercial is designed around two facts.
A scene cannot be unseen.
And people differ in resting asymmetry, a level each person carries into every task.
The answer is a mixed design, which compares some conditions between people and others within the same people.
The version of Commercial 1 is between subjects: each respondent sees only one version, because a viewer who has seen Version A, with the key scene, would watch Version B knowing what was cut.
Randomization, assignment by chance, decides who sees which, so that nothing about the people can line up systematically with the version.

The simulated plan assigns 48 respondents in blocks of four to four groups of 12 (Version A or B, each with Commercial 1 or Commercial 2 first); every block holds one respondent of each group, so the groups stay balanced even if collection stops early.
The demo study used the same logic on a small scale: two respondents saw Balls with the frog (Commercial 1 A), two saw it without (Commercial 1 B), and all four saw Paint (Commercial 2).
The commercials are within subjects: every respondent sees a version of Commercial 1 and also Commercial 2, and serves as his or her own control for H 3.

The first commercial can change how the second is received, through tiredness or knowing what the session holds, so counterbalancing shows each order to equal numbers of respondents within each version, and an effect of position falls equally on both commercials.
Each commercial also gets its own baseline, a neutral 60 seconds nature video just before it, and every score becomes a change score, the segment minus that baseline.
There are three reasons.
The iMotions notebook article says F A scores "should be interpreted relative to each other," and the fairest comparison is the same person a minute earlier.
Subtracting each person's resting level removes the trait and leaves the state, the shift that goes with what is on screen.
And a session drifts: the second commercial follows the first and a rating slide, so a fresh baseline limits the drift in its change score.
In the simulated data the two baselines average -0.052 and -0.054, correlate at r equals point 8 2, and 67.8 percent of baseline values are negative (all simulated).
Scores below zero are no problem, as in the demo chart, because only differences are interpreted.
The flow is therefore Baseline 1, the first commercial, a rating slide, Baseline 2, the second commercial, and a second rating slide.
The rating slide collects liking, the valence check that frontal asymmetry cannot supply.

The demo's baselines were "two 1-minute videos of fishes in a coral reef," and this plan copies their length; the lab manual describes longer eyes open and eyes closed rest periods for E E G (3 minutes of each in one place, 2.5 in another), so section 10 lists 60 seconds as a limitation.
Length matters for asymmetry.
By default the notebook cuts the E E G into windows 1 seconds long, a new one starting every 0.5 seconds (the Welch method, section 06), finds alpha power in each, and averages.
A 60 seconds commercial holds 119 windows, the 10 seconds end scene 19, and a 6 seconds key scene only 11.

An artifact, a voltage from a source other than the brain such as a blink or a clenched jaw, is often far larger than the brain signal, and a window with a sample above the artifact threshold is dropped, so short scenes give noisy averages.
In the simulated data the key scene change varies more between people than the whole commercial change (standard deviation 0.142 against 0.098, simulated).
A scene level hypothesis needs a scene long enough to hold several windows, respondents who blink normally and sit still, and more respondents than a whole commercial test.
Power analysis sets the sample before the data exist.
Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it is real; the usual target is 80 percent.
Within subjects the effect size is d z, the mean of the change scores divided by their standard deviation.
Between subjects it is d, the difference between group means divided by the pooled standard deviation, and the price rises sharply, because differences between people stay in the comparison.
In plain words.
Within subjects, at two tailed alpha point 0 5 and 80 percent power, a large effect (d z equals 0.8) needs 15 usable respondents, a medium one (0.5) 34, and a small one (0.3) 90.
Between subjects, a large effect (d equals 0.8) needs 26 per group and a medium one (0.5) 64 per group.
In the simulated study the end scene effect between versions was d equals 0.36, which needs 120 per version, while the key scene effect, d z equals 0.68, needs only 19 (simulated).
The same calculations in G*Power Means: difference between two dependent means (matched pairs), two tails, d z equals 0.5, alpha point 0 5, power point 8 0: total sample size 34.
Means: difference between two independent means (two groups), two tails, d equals 0.5, alpha point 0 5, power point 8 0, allocation ratio 1: 64 per group.
G*Power is the program most researchers cite.
The labels small, medium, and large were written for group differences, a rough guide for d z.
Two consequences follow.

A study of 48 must decide in advance which hypothesis it can test well: 24 per version is enough for H 1 if the key scene effect is near d z equals 0.7, and far too few for H 2 unless the version effect is very large, so the plan says beforehand that a nonsignificant H 2 will be inconclusive.
And H 1 uses only Version A, so its power depends on one group.
The table counts usable respondents, and losses fall on everyone scheduled, so divide the usable number by (1 minus the expected loss) and round up.

The simulated study lost 3 of 48 under its rule, about 6 percent, and would have lost 7, about 15 percent, under the stricter rule of its sensitivity analysis (simulated); a first study with a new protocol should plan for the higher figure.
For H 1 at d z equals 0.68 with 15 percent losses, 19 divided by 0.85 equals 22.4, so 23 per version.
Write the exclusion rule before anyone is recorded; a rule written after seeing the data is a rule chosen to get a result.

N I C 2 shows each electrode's contact as Red, Yellow, or Green, and each notebook report gives the Percentage of data filtered per channel, the share of samples removed at the artifact threshold (120 microvolts by default in the article text; the report screenshots name 100, so verify on the lab computer).

The rule: exclude a respondent when more than 25 percent of the F 3 or F 4 samples are removed in any baseline or commercial, or when the session log records a Red status at F 3 or F 4 that could not be fixed before recording.
Yellow is allowed, and every reason goes in the log.
One commercial pair is two stimuli, not a sample of commercials.
A difference between the commercials belongs to everything that differs at once, and a key scene effect to this scene in this commercial.
A claim about key scenes or commercials in general needs many of them analyzed as a sample, called stimulus sampling.
Last, preparation, consent, and comfort.

Oil, dead skin, and sweat raise the impedance, the resistance between electrode and scalp that N I C 2's colors summarize, so the lab manual asks respondents to wash their hair the night before with no conditioner or hair products, to avoid caffeine and heavy exercise for 2 hours before, and to sleep 7 hours or more, and it screens for gel allergies, seizure disorders, and photosensitivity.

Informed consent is a documented explanation, given before participation, of the purpose, the right to stop at any time, how the data will be handled, and the risks; here it names E E G as the signal recorded and explains that a snug cap is fitted and gel applied at each electrode.
Two articles set out the ethical questions: the neuroethics of neuromarketing and the ethical implications of its use and potential misuse.
The lab's own rules are simple: E E G files are personal data kept under respondent codes, and no result is ever described as reading a mind.
At Jacksonville State a study that will be published or presented first goes to the Institutional Review Board (I R B), the committee that reviews research with human participants.

Defend a mixed design with the version between subjects and the commercials within subjects, explain why each commercial gets its own baseline and why short scenes give noisy scores, size the sample for the hypothesis that needs it with losses included, and fix the exclusion rule, preparation, screening, and consent in advance.
The worked example in full
Everything in sections 01 and 02 fits on one page, the first deliverable of any study in this lab.
Below is the frontal asymmetry test as a student study plan; read it as a template for your own.

Among adult viewers, does the key scene in Commercial 1 shift F A toward approach relative to each viewer's resting level; is the end scene, where the brand appears, met with more approach after the version with the key scene than after the version without it; and do the two commercials differ in the shift they produce?
H 1: in Version A, F A during the key scene is higher than during the baseline before the commercial.
H 2: the baseline corrected end scene F A of Commercial 1 is higher in Version A than in Version B.
H 3: the baseline corrected whole commercial F A differs between Commercial 2 and Commercial 1.
Exploratory: liking, recall, frontal midline theta.
All tests two tailed at alpha point 0 5; H 1 and H 2 are supported only when significant in the predicted direction.
Mixed: version (A with the key scene, B without) between subjects; commercial within subjects, order counterbalanced within each version.
48 respondents (P 01 to P 48) assigned in blocks of four to four groups of 12: A C1first, A C2first, B C1first, B C2first.
An instruction slide, Baseline 1 (60 seconds nature video), the first commercial, a rating slide, Baseline 2 (a second 60 seconds nature video), the second commercial, a rating slide.
Commercial 1A: 60 seconds, key scene at 32.0 to 38.0 seconds.
Commercial 1B: 54 seconds, the same commercial with those 6 seconds cut.
Commercial 2: 60 seconds.
Two stimulus annotations: KeyScene (32.0 to 38.0 seconds of Commercial 1A only) and EndScene (the last 10 seconds of each commercial).
One Neuroelectrics Enobio 8 at a sampling rate of 500 hertz, gel at every electrode, U S B connection (iMotions recommends U S B, the lab manual describes Wi-Fi: verify the lab's choice).
N I C 2 protocol loaded with L S L Server on; in iMotions, a Lab Streaming Layer device named "Enobio E E G" with the Enobio device profile selected before the first recording.
channel 1 F z, channel 2 C z, channel 3 P z, channel 4 O z, channel 5 F 3, channel 6 F 4, channel 7 P 3, channel 8 P 4: ASSUMED from the lab manual's example montage.
Read the real map from the N I C 2 protocol on the lab computer and write it down before the first respondent.

E E G Frontal Asymmetry R Notebook: Left frontal electrode set channel 5 (F 3) and Right frontal electrode set channel 6 (F 4), entered by hand, never the defaults channel 1 and channel 7 (if the L S L Left and L S L Right frontal electrode set fields apply to the Enobio instead, enter the same channels there; verify which).

Alpha band (8 to 12 hertz); Welch P S D (50 percent overlap) with 1 seconds windows; band-pass filter 0.5 to 100 hertz; notch filter 60 hertz; artifact threshold 120 microvolts (the article's default; verify against the 100 named in the report screenshots).
Primary: Mean Frontal Asymmetry Alpha (E E G Frontal Asymmetry Metrics export) for each stimulus and annotation, as a change score from the baseline before the commercial.
Data quality: the Percentage of data filtered at F 3 and F 4 in each notebook report, and the N I C 2 status at F 3 and F 4 in the session log.

Exploratory: liking (1 to 7), key scene recall, brand naming, and Mean P S D channel 1 Theta (decibels), frontal midline theta at channel 1 (assumed F z), from the E E G Power Spectral Density R Notebook.

Exclude a respondent when more than 25 percent of the F 3 or F 4 samples are removed in any baseline or commercial, or when the session log records a Red status at F 3 or F 4 that could not be fixed before recording; log the reason.
H 1: a paired t test of the key scene against its baseline, with d z and its 95 percent confidence interval and a Wilcoxon signed rank test as a check.
H 2: Welch's t test, Version A against B, with Hedges' g, a Mann Whitney test, and the sample a conclusive test would need.

H 3: a paired t test, plus a mixed model with commercial, version, their interaction, viewing position, and a random intercept per respondent, with the I C C. Sensitivity analyses: a 15 percent exclusion threshold and no baseline correction.
Teaching contrast: H 1 with the default channels.

A table of F A change by segment and version, four figures, a results section and a discussion in journal form, and a three sentence client summary that says "shifted toward approach," never "liked" or "will buy."
Several names return in section 08.
An annotation marks a stretch of a timeline, and a stimulus annotation applies to everyone who saw that video.

Welch's t test compares two groups without assuming equal spread; the Wilcoxon and Mann Whitney tests repeat the paired and two group tests on ranks; the mixed model is a regression that knows which rows come from the same respondent; and a sensitivity analysis repeats a test under another reasonable choice.
Each hypothesis has one window.
H 1 uses the KeyScene of Version A against the baseline before Commercial 1A.
H 2 uses the EndScene of Commercial 1: its 10 seconds are the same footage in both versions, so a difference there can only come from what came before.
H 3 uses whole commercials, which share no scene and give the steadiest scores.
Liking is the valence check that F A cannot supply; theta is described, not tested.
The real material is the iMotions demo study "DEMO - Sony Bravia" in the Library on the lab computer (Lab - Alien).

Captures from October 10, 2026 show four respondents, R1 to R4; Baseline 1 and Baseline 2 (1 min each); Commercial 1A Balls (2 min 30 seconds, two respondents), Commercial 1B Balls (2 min 30 seconds), and Commercial 2 Paint (1 min 11 seconds), each followed by a rating slide; welcome, instruction, loading, and thank you slides; and a scene, Commercial 1A Balls and Frog, that isolates the frog.

The Sensors tab lists Eye tracking (Aurora), Respondent Camera (aff decks unticked), and Lab Streaming Layer; the Study settings Description holds the two Ohme references; and the Recorded Data tab offers Exposure summaries (Calculate) and Affectiva (Post Process).
The demo article (version 9.0) adds the rest.

Inspired by the two Ohme articles of 2010, the demo uses the Sony Bravia commercials Balls (2005) and Paint (2006): two respondents saw Balls with the frog scene (Commercial 1 A), two saw it without (Commercial 1 B), and all four saw Paint (Commercial 2), so 1 A and 1 B are compared between subjects and commercials 1 and 2 within subjects.
Its E E G came from an Enobio 32, whose channel numbers do not match the lab's Enobio 8.
Its example analysis compared "the last 10 seconds of the commercial," the end scene with the slogan "colours like no other," with the 1 minute baselines.
All its F A bars were negative, and Paint showed "a relatively stronger approach motivation (that is, less negative, hence more positive, frontal alpha asymmetry scores)" than Balls.
The article then warns that "more than four respondents would be needed to draw statistically relevant conclusions; this analysis is merely an example."
The article lists a Biopac unit for skin conductance that the lab copy's Sensors tab does not show.

The lab copy holds four saved analyses (Analysis, Analysis With FROG, Analysis Without FROG, and Baseline), and the first lists E E G Frontal Asymmetry flows, but when a new flow is started there the Devices list offers no E E G device and the R PROCESSING export tab lists no E E G export.
The lab copy therefore does not appear to hold E E G data the notebooks can process: use it to study the design, the stimuli, and the analysis setup, and use the simulated files for the numbers.

Wherever a number about respondents appears, it is simulated Every number about respondents in this workshop's analyses comes from a simulated data set built in the style of the demo study, shortened and enlarged for teaching.
No person was recorded, nothing about the Sony commercials went into it, and no number may be quoted as a finding.
The only real counts of people are the demo's four respondents.
One script, make simulated data dot P Y (seed 20267088), generated the six data files; each opens with lines that say simulated, and all share Respondent Name (P 01 to P 48).

simulated eeg fa metrics dot C S V is the file the tests use: one row per respondent and stimulus or annotation, 312 rows (seven per Version A respondent, six per Version B respondent, since only Commercial 1A has a KeyScene).

Its columns copy the E E G Frontal Asymmetry Metrics export in the R Processed E E G Export Files article with only Alpha selected: Study Name, Respondent Name, Gender, Age, Group (version and order, such as A C1first), Type, Label, Start (milliseconds), Duration (milliseconds), Parent Stimulus (which tells the three EndScene rows apart), Mean Frontal Asymmetry Alpha, and Algorithm Device Name.
Modeled, so check them in a pilot export: the Type values, Parent Stimulus on stimulus rows, and Algorithm Device Name as one column.

simulated eeg fa metrics default channels dot C S V is the same export run with the Enobio defaults, channel 1 and channel 7 (F z and P 3 under the assumed map), a teaching contrast never to be analyzed as asymmetry.

simulated eeg psd metrics dot C S V follows the E E G Power Spectral Density Metrics export with Theta and Alpha, from Mean P S D channel 1 Theta (decibels) to the Electrode Cluster Average; its column order and decibel base are modeled.
Three files are lab designs with modeled layouts.

simulated eeg artifact report dot C S V gives, per respondent, stimulus, and channel channel 5 (F 3) or channel 6 (F 4), the samples expected, recorded, and removed and the Percent removed ( percent), as copied from the report box Percentage of data filtered (nb of samples filtered divided by nb total of samples); verify whether that box gives values per stimulus.
simulated eeg session log dot C S V is the operator's log: cap size, connection, N I C 2 status at F 3 and F 4, gel, setup minutes, incidents, and a decision note.
simulated eeg survey dot C S V holds Liking Commercial 1 1to7, Liking Commercial 2 1to7, KeyScene Recall (N A for Version B), and Brand Named Correctly.

Three log notes say exclude: P 27 (Version A), whose F 4 stayed Red after re-seating, gel twice, and a lead swap (41.78 percent of F 4 removed in Commercial 1A); P 41 (Version A), with an 8.6 seconds L S L stream gap in Commercial 2 and then drift (30.42 percent of F 4 removed); and P 45 (Version B), with heavy movement and blinking (30.64 percent of F 3 removed in Commercial 1B).
That leaves 45, 22 in Version A and 23 in Version B (all simulated).
The folder also holds analysis.
R with its output and results tables, the workbook simulated eeg analysis dot X L S X with its walkthrough, and results text dot M D, the model paragraphs for sections 06, 09, and 10.

Write the one page plan for a frontal asymmetry study, pair each hypothesis with its window and change score, say what is and is not known about DEMO - Sony Bravia, name the simulated file that answers each question and the parts that are modeled or assumed, and explain why four respondents can test nothing.
Connecting the Enobio and building the study
An E E G (electroencephalography) recording, the record of tiny voltage changes picked up by electrodes (small sensors that touch the scalp), reaches iMotions through three programs.
The Enobio sends its signal to N I C 2, the Neuroelectrics control program (the manuals also write N I C and N I C 2).
N I C 2 publishes it on Lab Streaming Layer (L S L), "a universal system for synchronizing streaming data for live analysis or recording" in the iMotions L S L article.
iMotions listens through a Lab Streaming Layer device in Global Settings, and a study records it only if its sensors include Lab Streaming Layer.
Both lab license keys include the E E G and L S L modules.
Every link must hold before the first respondent arrives.
Why.

From brain waves to asymmetry: filters, power, the F A formula, and what to report
Every frontal asymmetry result ends a chain.

The electrodes of the Enobio 8 record scalp voltage 500 times per second, an R Notebook (a script that runs inside iMotions) cleans the signal and measures alpha power at a left and a right frontal electrode, and a formula turns the two powers into one score.
A methods section describes every link, following the publication guidelines for E E G studies and two primers on the road from raw signals to asymmetry scores.
E E G normally stays within about -100 to 100 microvolts around its mean (F A and P S D articles).
Artifacts, voltage from blinks, jaw muscles, movement, a lost contact, or the 60 hertz line noise of the building's power, can be far larger.
Both E E G notebooks clean the signal in the same order (P S D article):
a "zero phase-lag" band-pass filter, which keeps the frequencies inside a range, 0.5 to 100 hertz by default, without shifting the signal in time;
a zero phase-lag notch filter, which removes one narrow frequency: 60 hertz in the United States (the default), 50 hertz in Europe;
re-referencing, "for BrainProducts E E G only," so not for the Enobio;
an artifact threshold, 120 microvolts by default, "rejecting data-points whose absolute values exceed a preset voltage threshold."
The threshold catches large artifacts only; smaller blinks and muscle activity pass through.
The report screenshots name 100 microvolts instead of 120, so record the value in the panel and verify it on the lab machine.
In plain words.
A short stretch of E E G mixes waves of different speeds.
The fast Fourier transform (F F T) splits the stretch into the amount of each frequency, the way a prism splits light into colors.
The result is a power spectral density (P S D), how much power the signal carries at each frequency.
A frequency band is a named range of frequencies, and alpha power is the average P S D inside the alpha band, 8 to 12 hertz.

Welch's method and the legacy methodThe default Welch method, the "standard method in the scientific literature," cuts the signal into 1 seconds Hamming windows that overlap by 50 percent, giving one spectrum every 0.5 seconds, and drops any window that touches the threshold.
The legacy method, inspired by the A B M algorithm, averages three 1 seconds windows inside each 2 seconds window.
The Welch window can be 0.5, 1, or 2 seconds: "Only change this parameter if you know what you are doing."

Band power is then shown in decibels (decibels), a logarithmic unit, and averaging "across electrodes, time and participants is performed before applying any logarithmic transform" (P S D article).
The order matters, because the log of an average is not the average of the logs: averaging exported decibels values yourself will not reproduce the notebook's aggregate (this workshop's inference).
Whether the F A notebook averages window F A values or window powers is not stated; verify on the lab machine.
In words, the notebook subtracts "the natural logarithm transformed alpha power in the left hemisphere from the natural logarithm transformed alpha power in the right hemisphere."

The natural logarithm (natural log) turns a ratio into a difference, the natural log of (right divided by left) equals the natural log of (right) minus the natural log of (left), and it is zero when the two powers are equal.
The result is frontal alpha asymmetry (F A; the article also writes F A A), computed in every window and exported as a mean per stimulus and per annotation.
In plain words"Alpha power is inversely related to the level of brain activity," the F A article says: less alpha on one side means more activity there.
So when right alpha is stronger than left alpha, the left side is relatively more active and F A is positive.

A positive or rising F A means relatively more left frontal activity, read as approach motivation, the urge to move toward something; a negative or falling F A means relatively more right frontal activity, read as withdrawal motivation, the urge to move away.

This section runs the planned tests on the simulated exports, in R with analysis dot R (output in analysis output dot T X T) and then in Excel.
Every statistic is simulated and matches that output exactly.
Frontal asymmetry (F A) is in natural log units throughout.
The F A export has 312 rows for 48 respondents: 7 per Version A respondent (two baselines, two commercials, KeyScene, two EndScene rows) and 6 per Version B respondent.

Its column names are the manual's; the Type values, Parent Stimulus on stimulus rows, the single Algorithm Device Name column, and the layouts of the artifact report, session log, and survey are modeled, so verify them on the lab machine.
Because the annotation label EndScene appears on every commercial, a row is identified by Label and Parent Stimulus together.

The script confirms that every annotation lies inside its parent stimulus, that EndScene starts 10000 milliseconds before the end of its commercial and KeyScene 32000 milliseconds into Commercial 1A, and that the three exports have identical rows.

One check links two exports: the simulated P S D export writes decibels as 10 log10 of power (a modeled choice; the manuals do not state the base), so 4.343 decibels equals one natural log unit, and F A recomputed as (channel 6 alpha decibels minus channel 5 alpha decibels) divided by 4.343 agreed with the exported F A, r equals point 9 9 4 over 292 rows (simulated).

The rule, written before collection: exclude a respondent when more than 25 percent of the F 3 or F 4 samples were removed by the artifact threshold in any baseline or commercial (artifact report), or when the session log records a Red N I C 2 status at F 3 or F 4 that could not be fixed.
It removed three (simulated):
P 27 (Version A): F 4 stayed Red after re-seating, gel twice, and a lead swap; 41.78 percent of F 4 removed in Commercial 1A.
Its F A values, 0.630 to 0.762, lay outside the kept range, -0.357 to 0.385.
P 41 (Version A): an L S L stream gap of about 8.6 seconds in Commercial 2, then drift; 30.42 percent of F 4 and 28.90 percent of F 3 removed.
P 45 (Version B): heavy movement and blinking; 30.64 percent of F 3 removed in Commercial 1B.
That leaves 45 respondents, 22 in Version A and 23 in Version B.

In the kept rows the median percentage removed was 1.46 (90th percentile 6.01, maximum 22.83); nine kept respondents had a Red status fixed before recording, and 19 of 48 were recorded with Yellow, which the rule allows.
The respondent, not the row, is the unit of analysis.

Baseline F A was M equals -0.052 (standard deviation equals 0.130) for Baseline 1 and M equals -0.054 (standard deviation equals 0.128) for Baseline 2, t(44) equals -0.21, p equals point 8 3 4, and a respondent's two baselines correlated r equals point 8 2 (simulated): comparable baselines, and a stable personal level that the change score removes.
Each commercial is compared with the baseline right before it, which depends on the order: Baseline 1 for Commercial 1 in a C1first respondent, Baseline 2 in a C2first respondent.
In plain words.
For each Version A respondent, subtract the F A in the baseline before Commercial 1A from the F A during the key scene, the 6 seconds scene only Version A contains.
If the scene changed nothing, these changes would average about zero.
A one sample t test on the changes, the same as a paired t test, asks whether their average is far from zero relative to how much they vary.

F A rose from -0.090 (standard deviation 0.104) to 0.008 (standard deviation 0.157), and 17 of 22 respondents were higher during the scene (simulated).
The effect size d z, the mean change divided by the standard deviation of the changes, was 0.68, 95 percent confidence interval 0.21 to 1.14, from the noncentral t distribution.
The Wilcoxon signed rank test, which ranks the changes instead of assuming normality, agreed (V equals 210, p equals point 0 0 7), and a Shapiro Wilk test of normality gave p equals point 8 2 1.
H 1 was supported.

The key scene change was noisier than the whole commercial change (standard deviation 0.142 against 0.098) and correlated less with its baseline (r equals point 4 6 against point 6 3): 11 windows average out less noise than 119.
Different people saw the two versions, so H 2 is a between subjects comparison of the baseline corrected F A in the end scene, the last 10 seconds of Commercial 1, where the brand appears.
Welch's t test compares two independent groups without assuming equal variances, the recommended default.

Version A was higher, 0.033 (standard deviation 0.124) against -0.012 (standard deviation 0.123), a difference of 0.045, 95 percent confidence interval -0.029 to 0.119, but Welch t(42.87) equals 1.22, p equals point 2 2 9 (simulated).

Hedges' g, the difference in pooled standard deviation units with a small sample correction, was 0.36, 95 percent confidence interval -0.22 to 0.94, and the Mann Whitney test, the rank based check for two groups, agreed (W equals 313, p equals point 1 7 7).
H 2 was not supported.
The interval runs from a small reversal to a large effect, so the result is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect.

A power analysis, how likely a design is to detect an effect of a given size, shows why: at d equals 0.36 a new study needs 120 respondents per version (240 in total) for 80 percent power, and with 22 and 23 the power was 0.22.
A within subjects test at the H 1 effect size (d z equals 0.68) needs 19, because it removes the differences between people from the error term.

H 3 compares the whole commercial changes within all 45 respondents: Commercial 1 to 0.029 (standard deviation 0.081), Commercial 2 0.004 (standard deviation 0.085), a difference of 0.033, 95 percent confidence interval -0.001 to 0.066, paired t(44) equals 1.98, p equals point 0 5 5, d z equals 0.29, 95 percent confidence interval -0.01 to 0.59 (simulated).

The plan named the paired t test, so it is the test of H 3, and H 3 was not supported at point 0 5; the Wilcoxon result is reported as the check, and the estimate with its interval says what is known: a small difference, measured imprecisely.

Simulation.
The data follow planned effects; they demonstrate the analysis, not the effect.
The channel map.
Only the N I C 2 protocol says which site each of channel 1 to channel 8 holds.
The map was assumed, and the default channel contrast showed that a wrong pair erases the key scene effect with no warning in the export.
The map, the reference, and the electrode sets belong in every methods section.
A short window.

The 6 seconds key scene gives about 11 one second windows against 119 for a whole commercial, and its change was noisier (standard deviation 0.142 against 0.098); short scenes need more respondents, longer windows, or repeated exposures.
Between subjects power.
H 2 was a between subjects comparison; a conclusive test at the observed effect would need about 120 respondents per version, more than five times the present sample.
Two baselines.
The second baseline follows a commercial and a rating slide, drift over the session enters the change score, and 60 seconds is shorter than the baseline periods in the lab manual.
One pair of commercials.
The results describe these stimuli; general claims need several stimuli treated as a random factor.
The artifact rule.

The 120 microvolt threshold leaves smaller blinks and muscle activity in the frontal channels, the manuals give both 120 and 100, and the artifact report is a modeled table; the 15 percent sensitivity analysis changed no conclusion.
F A is relative and depends on processing.
Scores carry meaning only against each other and depend on choices such as the reference and the electrode pair.

A respondent's two baselines correlated r equals point 8 2: much of an asymmetry score is a stable, trait like level that the person brings to the session, and a smaller part is the state that a commercial changes.
The change score removes the trait, which is why the I C C of the change scores was only point 1 1 0.
Whether scores are dependable enough to compare moments is a reliability question; see Towers and Allen (2009) on estimating the internal consistency of asymmetry scores.
Each sensor answers a different question on the same timeline.
Eye tracking (Workshop 2) shows what each viewer was looking at during the key scene, so an F A change can be read against whether the scene was seen.
Facial expression analysis (Workshop 3) adds expressed valence, the pleasant or unpleasant direction F A does not give.
Skin conductance (Workshop 4) adds arousal, the intensity of the response.

The Sony Bravia demo was designed with a survey, eye tracking, facial expression analysis, electrodermal activity, and E E G; the lab copy's Sensors tab lists Eye tracking (Aurora), Respondent Camera, and Lab Streaming Layer, so check on the lab computer which data it holds.
Whether brain measures predict the market is an open question.

Studies have reported that brain responses to movie trailers predict individual preferences and population wide commercial success and have combined neurophysiological methods with market response modeling to predict advertising success (Venkatraman and colleagues
, 2015); for the field see Smidts and colleagues (2014) and the critical review of branding research by Plassmann and colleagues (2012).
This workshop's advice: pair F A with a criterion such as recall, choice, or sales, and treat F A alone as a measure of approach, not of success.

Intersubject correlation would show whether viewers' E E G moved together during the key scene, a group score that needs at least two valid respondents; audience preferences have been reported to be predicted by the temporal reliability of neural processing (Dmochowski and colleagues
Frontal midline theta could show whether a scene demanded more processing, the approach of the workload article built on M. E. Smith and colleagues
(2001); iMotions has no separate workload notebook, so it is the P S D notebook with the band and channel set by hand.
Neither measures motivation, and both need their own hypotheses.

A preregistration, a time stamped plan filed before the first respondent, records the channel map and how it was verified, the electrode sets, bands, window, and threshold, the exclusion rule, the baseline correction, the annotation windows, the tests with their direction, and the sample size with its power reasoning.
A replication would add commercials as a stimulus sample and size the between subjects comparison for a realistic effect.
The report follows the general reporting standards and the E E G guidelines (Keil and colleagues
, 2014), including every exclusion with its rule, value, and reason.
Recording brain activity for marketing raises its own questions, set out in work on the neuroethics of neuromarketing and on its ethical implications and potential misuse.

At Jacksonville State a study that will be published or presented goes first to the I R B, and every session needs informed consent that names the cap and gel, the E E G recording, the screening questions (gel allergy, seizure disorders, photosensitivity), and how long the data are kept.
